screens.title: What is VEX and why use it?
screens.narratorSegment: VEX, short for Vector Expression Language, is Houdini's lightweight, high-performance language for manipulating geometry data and attributes. At its core, VEX is designed to run a small program repeatedly across many elements — points, primitives, vertices, or the whole detail — so you can express per-element behavior concisely and efficiently. Think of VEX as a compact, typed scripting language similar in style to C or JavaScript but focused on vector math and geometry operations. A key feature is the ability to refer to attributes directly using the at symbol, which lets the running instance read or write the attribute of the current element. For example, when you write an expression that changes position, that code runs separately for every point and modifies that point's position only. The efficiency of VEX makes it practical to perform complex procedural transformations on large datasets where node-only setups would be cumbersome. A common misconception is that VEX is only for advanced users; in reality, small VEX snippets often replace multi-node setups and give precise control. Now imagine you need each point to offset upward by a small amount; VEX does this with a single-line change and executes it across the entire geometry. How might you use that same approach to drive color, normals, or exported attributes?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: VEX is a high-performance, element-wise language used to programmatically read and write geometry attributes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What is VEX?
VEX — a concise definition
VEX runs a program for each geometry component. It uses typed variables and direct attribute access to manipulate data efficiently.
Data types
float, int, vector, vector2, vector4, string and typed attribute prefixes like f@, i@, v@.
Attribute access
Use the at sign to read and write attributes such as @P, @Cd, @N in the running instance.
Performance
VEX is optimized for per-element execution and is preferable for large, repeated operations.
Concrete example
Move every point upward slightly by changing its y coordinate with a single VEX line.
Key takeaway
Small VEX programs replace many nodes and run efficiently across geometry.
Analogy
Treat VEX as a per-row formula in a spreadsheet: the same formula runs for each row, but it can read and write that row's values.
Common misconception
Learners often assume loops are required to process all points. The wrangle already executes per component, so loops are only needed for inner iteration within a single element's context.
Short code panel
// Move each point upward by 0.1
@P.y += 0.1;

// Assign a random color per point
@Cd = rand(@ptnum);

screens.title: Attribute Wrangle SOP — execution model
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the Attribute Wrangle's execution model is essential. The node provides a Run Over setting that tells Houdini whether your VEX code should execute once per point, per primitive, per vertex, or once for the detail. When Run Over is set to points, each invocation of your VEX code receives the context of a single point: built-in variables like @P and @ptnum refer to that point specifically. If you switch Run Over to primitives, @P is not directly meaningful and you instead work with primitive attributes and @primnum. This distinction explains many early errors learners encounter: code that references @P while running over primitives will fail. Another important detail is that declaring typed attributes such as f@myFloat in a wrangle will create that attribute at the chosen class — a point-level declaration inside a point wrangle creates a point attribute. Use the Group parameter on the node to limit which elements the VEX runs on. Common workflows start with Run Over set to points for per-point displacement and color, then change to primitives or detail when aggregating or writing single values for the entire geometry. Always check the Geometry Spreadsheet after changes; it immediately shows whether attributes exist at the intended class and with the expected type.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Execution Model
Run Over: steps to reason about
Step 1
Choose Points, Primitives, Vertices or Detail. This decides which attributes are meaningful in the execution context.
Step 2
Write VEX that assumes the chosen class. For points, use @P and @ptnum; for primitives, use @primnum and primitive-specific attributes.
Step 3
Limit the run using the Group parameter to target subsets like a named group or expression-based mask.
Example
Point wrangle: change @P; Primitive wrangle: compute a per-primitive color and assign to primitive-level Cd.
Pitfall
Referencing @P while running over primitives will make @P unavailable and cause confusion or errors.
Visual process cards
Points
Per-point code; use @P, @ptnum, declare f@ and v@ for point attributes.
Primitives
Per-primitive code; use @primnum and primitive attributes.
Detail
Runs once for the whole geometry; useful for aggregates such as global counts.
Key takeaway
Match Run Over to the attributes you intend to access; check the spreadsheet to verify attribute class and type.

screens.title: Attribute access and typed declarations
screens.narratorSegment: In VEX you interact with attributes using the @ prefix. That symbol tells VEX you're referring to an attribute on the current running element. For example, @P references a point's position vector, @Cd the color, and @N the normal. When you write directly to an attribute the change is applied to that element during execution. Typed declarations let you create new attributes explicitly and ensure the correct type is stored. Prefixes such as f@ for float, i@ for integer, v@ for vector, and s@ for string are common. For example, writing f@myFloat = 0.5; creates a floating-point attribute named myFloat on the selected class. A common beginner error is assigning a single float to a vector attribute, such as attempting to write @Cd = 0.5; which fails—colors require vectors like {0.5,0.5,0.5}. Another useful pattern is to declare a typed custom attribute for export, such as i@custom_id = @ptnum;, which is handy when preparing geometry for game engines. Always confirm attribute types in the Geometry Spreadsheet; mismatched types are a frequent source of runtime confusion. Attribute access and typed declarations means use @ to access attributes and f@/v@/i@/s@ prefixes to declare attributes with explicit types for clarity and correctness.. In practical terms, how to read, write, and declare attributes with the @ prefix and f@/v@/i@ prefixes.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Attribute Access
Access patterns
Read
Use @name to read the current element's attribute value, for example @P or @Cd.
Write
Assign values to attributes directly: @P *= 2; or @Cd = {1,0,0};
Declare
Create typed attributes with prefixes: f@height, v@velocity, i@id, s@name.
Example
i@custom_id = @ptnum; creates an integer attribute storing the point index for export.
Common mistake
Assigning wrong types, such as @Cd = 0.5, will either error or produce an unexpected result. Use a vector for colors.
Quick code
// Declare a float and a vector attribute
f@height = 0.5;
v@myVec = {1, 0, 0};

// Create an exportable ID
i@custom_id = @ptnum;
Key takeaway
Be explicit with types. Use the Geometry Spreadsheet to confirm the attribute class and type after declaration.

screens.title: Basic VEX examples — move and color
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through two direct VEX examples that you will use frequently. The first is moving points upward: adding a small value to the y coordinate modifies each point's vertical position. This is expressed compactly in VEX and runs for every point when Run Over is set to points. The second example assigns color using a pseudo-random function seeded by the point number, which ensures each point receives a deterministic but varied value. When using rand, seed with a unique identifier such as the point index so results differ per element. Remember that rand returns a float between zero and one, and assigning it to the color attribute requires forming a vector. A typical beginner mistake is forgetting to wrap the single float as a vector. Using these two snippets together gives both spatial modification and visual feedback: if you change position and then assign colors, you'll immediately see the effect in the viewport. As you practice, try altering the random seed or the movement amount to see how small parameter changes produce large visual variety. In practical terms, simple snippets that change position and assign point colors.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Basic VEX Examples
Move points upward
// Move every point upward by 0.1
@P.y += 0.1;
This line modifies the running point's y coordinate directly. When combined with a parameter channel, you can scale this movement without changing code.
Example outcome
A grid will visibly rise and create displacement that you can visualize in the viewport.
Assign random color per point
// Random color using point number as seed
@Cd = rand(@ptnum);

// Ensure proper vector form when needed
@Cd = set(rand(@ptnum), rand(@ptnum+1), rand(@ptnum+2));
rand returns a float; using set or a vector literal ensures @Cd receives a vector. Seeding with different offsets produces RGB variety.
Key takeaway
Use deterministic seeds like @ptnum to create repeatable randomness across runs.

screens.title: ch(), rand(), fit() and set()
screens.narratorSegment: VEX contains a collection of small functions that make procedural work straightforward. The ch function is particularly useful because it creates a parameter on the wrangle node that you can adjust in the UI. For example, creating a channel for scale allows you to multiply positions without editing the VEX each time. rand generates pseudo-random numbers between zero and one and is commonly seeded with an index like the point number. fit remaps values from one numeric range to another; you'll often use it to convert a position range into a normalized 0-to-1 scale. The set function constructs vectors from separate floats, which is practical when you want to assign RGB values from different random calls. Together these functions let you expose artist parameters, add variety, and normalize data for driving attributes. A simple pattern is to ch a scale, use fit to remap a coordinate to a 0–1 blend, and feed that into a color calculation seeded with rand. Remember to type your attributes correctly when using these functions: fit returns a float, set produces a vector, and ch returns the parameter type you requested on the node.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Key Functions
ch() — exposed parameter
Create a node parameter you can tweak without editing code. Useful for artist control and iterative testing.
Pattern
float scale = ch('scale_factor'); @P *= scale;
rand(), fit(), set()
rand produces floats; fit remaps ranges; set constructs vectors from floats for color or position components.
// remap Y from -0.5..0.5 to 0..1
float t = fit(@P.y, -0.5, 0.5, 0, 1);
// color from random seeds
@Cd = set(rand(@ptnum), rand(@ptnum+1), rand(@ptnum+2));
Concrete example
Use ch to expose a scale slider, fit to remap a Y position into that slider's domain, and rand to seed color variation — this produces a controllable, visually varied result.

screens.title: If/Else and simple for loops in VEX
screens.narratorSegment: Control flow in VEX lets you branch logic and perform internal repetitions. The if/else statement allows you to change attributes only when certain conditions hold, such as coloring points red when their Y position is above a threshold and blue otherwise. This is especially powerful when combined with fit or other remapping functions to create bands or ramps. Loops, like for loops, are less common at the per-element level because the wrangle itself iterates across elements, but they are useful within a single execution for tasks like averaging or sampling neighboring elements. For instance, you might loop a fixed number of times to accumulate nearby attributes into an average and then write that average to a custom attribute. A key misconception is thinking you must loop over all points; instead, plan whether the wrangle should run per point and do inner loops only for local aggregation. Always be careful with loop bounds to avoid expensive or unintended work on large geometries. Structuring conditions and internal loops with clear comments and small, predictable ranges keeps VEX fast and maintainable. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Conditionals & Loops
if / else example
// Color points based on Y threshold
if (@P.y > 0.5) {
  @Cd = {1, 0, 0};
} else {
  @Cd = {0, 0, 1};
}
This clearly separates the two color branches and is easy to read and debug in the spreadsheet.
for loop use-case
// Average a small fixed set of values inside one execution
float sum = 0;
for (int i=0; i<4; i++) {
  sum += rand(@ptnum + i);
}
float avg = sum / 4.0;
f@local_avg = avg;
Use loops for bounded internal work. Avoid large or unbounded loops on per-element code to keep performance predictable.
Concrete example
Use if/else to separate tall and short points, then compute a nearby-sample average with a small fixed for loop to smooth values.
Check your understanding
Why would you avoid a loop that iterates over all points inside a point wrangle? Think performance and duplication of outer loop work.

screens.title: Grid hands-on: scale by Y and assign random color
screens.narratorSegment: Follow a reproducible hands-on pattern. Start with a grid set to fifty rows and columns. Add an Attribute Wrangle and set Run Over to points. In the wrangle create a float channel named scale_intensity and read it with ch. Then remap the point's Y position with fit to a desired scale range and multiply positions by the remapped value and the channel. Next assign a random color per point by seeding rand with the point number. Finally create an integer attribute to store a custom id using the point index, which is useful when exporting. After the wrangle, add a Color SOP set to read From Attributes so you can visualize the color attribute, and add a Normal SOP to restore normals after scaling. Use the Geometry Spreadsheet to confirm that Cd and custom_id exist and have the expected types. This step-by-step gives you a controlled, adjustable result you can tweak instantly from the node UI without editing code each time. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Hands-on Grid
Starter VEX (visual)
// Create a channel
float scale_intensity = ch('scale_intensity');

// Remap Y and scale
float y_scale = fit(@P.y, -0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.5);
@P *= y_scale * scale_intensity;

// Assign random color
@Cd = rand(@ptnum);

// Add ID for export
i@custom_id = @ptnum;
Adjust scale_intensity on the node to see immediate changes. Add a Color SOP After the wrangle to pick Color Type: From Attributes, and add a Normal SOP to recalculate normals.
Checklist
  • Grid: Rows and Columns = 50
  • Wrangle: Run Over = Points
  • Use ch to expose scale_intensity
  • Verify Cd and custom_id in Geometry Spreadsheet
Real-world benefit
This pattern produces an adjustable procedural surface that exports per-point metadata for downstream tools.

screens.title: Common mistakes and debugging strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners often encounter a few recurring issues. One is forgetting the at symbol when referencing attributes; without it you reference a local variable instead of the attribute, producing wrong results or undefined behavior. Another common error is mixing types — for example assigning a float to a vector attribute. Always ensure you provide the correct shape: colors need vectors, while scalars require float or int types. A third issue is Run Over mismatch: if your code expects per-point context but the node is running over primitives, attributes like @P won't be meaningful. Debugging strategies include using the Geometry Spreadsheet to inspect attribute existence and types, inserting temporary attributes with clear names to confirm intermediate values, and creating ch channels to test parameter changes without editing code. When a random seed doesn't change results as expected, try offsetting the seed or adding a ch('seed') parameter. Finally, comment your VEX and test small, incremental changes rather than large rewrites. These habits reduce errors and make it easier to identify whether a problem is a type, scope, or logic error. Common mistakes and debugging strategies means use the geometry spreadsheet and small, incremental tests to find missing @, type mismatches, and run over issues quickly.. In practical terms, avoid type errors, missing @, and run over mismatches; use the geometry spreadsheet.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Checklist of common mistakes
  • Missing the @ prefix when referencing attributes.
  • Assigning wrong types, e.g., float to a vector attribute.
  • Incorrect Run Over setting (points vs primitives vs detail).
  • Unbounded loops inside per-element execution causing slowdowns.
Pitfall example
Attempting @Cd = 0.5; will not produce valid RGB—use a vector form instead.
Strategies to verify
Open Geometry Spreadsheet and check attribute names, classes, and types after running the wrangle.
Expose temporary channels with ch to adjust values interactively and watch results change.
Write intermediate attributes such as f@debugVal to capture expressions for inspection.
Key takeaway
Small tests and the spreadsheet are the fastest way to find whether a problem is syntactic, type-related, or a Run Over mismatch.

screens.title: Integrating wrangles into a procedural network
screens.narratorSegment: When building a procedural network, treat the Attribute Wrangle as a compact, maintainable module. Keep wrangles focused—one for displacement, one for color, one for export attributes—so each node has a single responsibility. Use ch channels to expose only the parameters you expect artists to edit. After making geometric changes, recalculate normals with a Normal SOP so shading remains consistent. When colors or custom data must be visualized, add a Color SOP set to From Attributes. For exported metadata, declare typed attributes explicitly and perform a final check in the Geometry Spreadsheet before writing out. If you need aggregation, run a detail wrangle or a primitive wrangle after per-point work to compute global values. Comment your VEX and use descriptive attribute names like i@custom_id or f@height_scale so downstream artists and tools know intent. This modular, named-attribute approach keeps procedural trees understandable and simplifies debugging and iteration in larger projects. Integrating wrangles into a procedural network means use small focused wrangles, expose parameters with ch, recalc normals, and verify attributes before export for clean procedural pipelines.. In practical terms, patterns for readable, exportable attribute workflows and downstream sops.. Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Network Patterns
Modular wrangle pattern
Split responsibilities: displacement wrangle, color wrangle, export wrangle. Keep each node small and documented so you can re-order or bypass nodes during iteration.
Expose a limited set of ch parameters for artists to control without editing code.
After geometry changes, add a Normal SOP to maintain correct shading and a Color SOP to visualize Cd.
Use explicit attribute names for downstream clarity and export compatibility.
Concrete example
Wrangle A: scale points; Wrangle B: assign @Cd and i@custom_id; Normal SOP; Color SOP reading @Cd.
Key takeaway
Design wrangles as modular steps and verify with the spreadsheet to keep networks maintainable.

screens.title: Performance hints and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: VEX is fast, but performance still matters on large geometry sets. Avoid unbounded loops inside a per-element wrangle; looping over all points in each point execution duplicates work and multiplies cost. Prefer built-in functions which are optimized, and limit attribute writes to only those you need because every written attribute consumes memory and can slow later processing. Use temporary attributes for debugging but remove or hide them in final setups. When sampling neighbors, restrict the neighborhood size or use dedicated nodes for heavy topology queries rather than naive loops. Reuse computed values within a single execution instead of recomputing them. If you need global aggregates, perform them in a detail wrangle that runs once rather than in every point. Finally, test with smaller data sets and check timings before moving to full-resolution geometry; small prototypes reveal algorithmic issues faster than large runs. Following these steps keeps your procedural tools interactive and reliable in production pipelines. Practical rules
  • Avoid loops that iterate over all elements inside a per-element wrangle.
  • Use built-in functions and specialized SOPs for heavy topology work.

Testing strategy
Prototype on smaller grids, test timings, and profile expensive steps. If a calculation is global, move it to a detail wrangle to run once.
Key takeaway

screens.title: Assessment: random X-offset for a named group
screens.narratorSegment: A practical assessment checks your understanding of groups, randomness, and remapping. The task is to randomly offset the X position of points in a specific group called offset_points by a maximum of 0.2 units in either direction. The correct approach sets the Attribute Wrangle Group parameter to offset_points so only those points run. Inside the wrangle, use rand seeded with the point index plus a seed channel to allow variation, then use fit to remap the 0-to-1 random value to the range minus 0.2 to 0.2. Finally add that offset to @P. x. This uses ch to expose a seed parameter for reproducibility or animation. Key things to check are that only the group is affected, that the random values differ per point, and that the remapping produces both negative and positive offsets. A misconception is trying to filter with an if statement rather than using the node's Group parameter — using the Group is clearer and more efficient. Assessment: random X-offset for a named group means set group to the target, use rand seeded with @ptnum and ch seed, and fit to map random floats to [-0.2, 0.2] for x offsets.. In practical terms, apply rand and fit to offset points in a group by ±0.2 units using a seed channel.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Assessment
Assessment code (visual)
// Seeded random, remapped to -0.2..0.2
float offset_x = fit(rand(@ptnum + ch('seed')), 0, 1, -0.2, 0.2);
@P.x += offset_x;
Set the Group parameter on the wrangle to offset_points so only those points run. The ch seed parameter allows repeatable variation or animation control.
Checklist
  • Group: offset_points
  • Use rand with @ptnum + seed
  • Use fit to map to -0.2..0.2
Misconception
Avoid using an if inside a full-point run to filter points; using the Group parameter is clearer and more efficient.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize the essentials. First, VEX is a compact, fast language for writing per-element operations; it shines when you need procedural control over large geometry sets. Second, the Attribute Wrangle SOP runs your VEX across a chosen class—points, primitives, vertices, or detail—so match Run Over to the attributes you intend to access. Third, the at-prefixed attributes and typed declarations like f@, v@, i@ are how you read, write, and create attributes reliably. Fourth, ch, rand, fit, and set are practical functions for creating controllable parameters, seeded randomness, remapping ranges, and assembling vectors. Fifth, use the Geometry Spreadsheet and visualization SOPs to verify attribute existence and types. Finally, follow modular, small-wrangle patterns, avoid unbounded loops, expose only necessary channels, and comment your code to keep networks maintainable. These concepts give you a practical toolkit for building procedural effects that are controllable, debuggable, and efficient.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll meet VEX, Houdini's compact, high-performance expression language, and the Attribute Wrangle SOP, the node that runs your VEX code across geometry. You will learn how attributes like position, color, and normals are read and written using the @ prefix, how to declare typed attributes, and how common VEX functions let you create procedural behaviors. We will practice with a grid, showing how to move points, assign random colors, and expose parameters using ch so you can tweak values at the node level without editing code. Along the way you'll see conditional logic and simple loops, and I'll point out common pitfalls like mismatched types and the importance of the Run Over setting. By the end you'll be able to implement compact VEX snippets that create dynamic, data-driven effects and export attributes ready for downstream use. Try to keep an eye on the geometry spreadsheet while you code — it tells you whether attributes exist and have the expected types. Ready to open the wrangle and start coding? Consider what attribute you'd like to drive first: position, color, or a custom flag.

These objectives set the foundation for practical VEX use. First, you'll be introduced to VEX and how it functions as the language to operate on geometry attributes. You'll learn what makes VEX suited for per-component operations and how the wrangle node executes your code across points or primitives. Second, you'll understand the purpose of the Attribute Wrangle SOP: how it exposes a compact editor and the Run Over setting that determines execution context. Third, you'll practice writing basic expressions to access and modify attributes such as position, color, and normals using the @ prefix and typed declarations. Fourth, you'll begin using simple built-in functions that make attributes dynamic, like generating random values or remapping ranges. Together these skills let you create repeatable, adjustable procedural effects and verify them in the geometry spreadsheet. As you work, check that attribute types and the Run Over mode match your intent — that saves debugging time and prevents type mismatch errors.

This second objectives page focuses on applied skills and verification. You will practice implementing conditional logic like if and else so attributes change only when conditions are met. You will learn when and how to use simple for loops inside a single execution to iterate arrays or neighborhood data. You will learn to use ch to create adjustable parameters on the wrangle node for artist-friendly control, and how to wire that parameter into your VEX expressions. Finally, you'll learn to verify results using the Geometry Spreadsheet and visualizers such as a Color SOP or Normal SOP, and to avoid common mistakes like missing the @ prefix or assigning wrong types. Together these objectives ensure you can build procedural setups that are both controllable and debuggable in a production-style workflow. Learning Objectives — Part 2 means apply conditional logic, loops, and node channels, and verify attributes using the geometry spreadsheet and visualization sops.. In practical terms, applied skills, debugging, and patterns to verify results.. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

VEX, short for Vector Expression Language, is Houdini's lightweight, high-performance language for manipulating geometry data and attributes. At its core, VEX is designed to run a small program repeatedly across many elements — points, primitives, vertices, or the whole detail — so you can express per-element behavior concisely and efficiently. Think of VEX as a compact, typed scripting language similar in style to C or JavaScript but focused on vector math and geometry operations. A key feature is the ability to refer to attributes directly using the at symbol, which lets the running instance read or write the attribute of the current element. For example, when you write an expression that changes position, that code runs separately for every point and modifies that point's position only. The efficiency of VEX makes it practical to perform complex procedural transformations on large datasets where node-only setups would be cumbersome. A common misconception is that VEX is only for advanced users; in reality, small VEX snippets often replace multi-node setups and give precise control. Now imagine you need each point to offset upward by a small amount; VEX does this with a single-line change and executes it across the entire geometry. How might you use that same approach to drive color, normals, or exported attributes?

Understanding the Attribute Wrangle's execution model is essential. The node provides a Run Over setting that tells Houdini whether your VEX code should execute once per point, per primitive, per vertex, or once for the detail. When Run Over is set to points, each invocation of your VEX code receives the context of a single point: built-in variables like @P and @ptnum refer to that point specifically. If you switch Run Over to primitives, @P is not directly meaningful and you instead work with primitive attributes and @primnum. This distinction explains many early errors learners encounter: code that references @P while running over primitives will fail. Another important detail is that declaring typed attributes such as f@myFloat in a wrangle will create that attribute at the chosen class — a point-level declaration inside a point wrangle creates a point attribute. Use the Group parameter on the node to limit which elements the VEX runs on. Common workflows start with Run Over set to points for per-point displacement and color, then change to primitives or detail when aggregating or writing single values for the entire geometry. Always check the Geometry Spreadsheet after changes; it immediately shows whether attributes exist at the intended class and with the expected type.

In VEX you interact with attributes using the @ prefix. That symbol tells VEX you're referring to an attribute on the current running element. For example, @P references a point's position vector, @Cd the color, and @N the normal. When you write directly to an attribute the change is applied to that element during execution. Typed declarations let you create new attributes explicitly and ensure the correct type is stored. Prefixes such as f@ for float, i@ for integer, v@ for vector, and s@ for string are common. For example, writing f@myFloat = 0.5; creates a floating-point attribute named myFloat on the selected class. A common beginner error is assigning a single float to a vector attribute, such as attempting to write @Cd = 0.5; which fails—colors require vectors like {0.5,0.5,0.5}. Another useful pattern is to declare a typed custom attribute for export, such as i@custom_id = @ptnum;, which is handy when preparing geometry for game engines. Always confirm attribute types in the Geometry Spreadsheet; mismatched types are a frequent source of runtime confusion. VEX contains a collection of small functions that make procedural work straightforward. The ch function is particularly useful because it creates a parameter on the wrangle node that you can adjust in the UI. For example, creating a channel for scale allows you to multiply positions without editing the VEX each time. rand generates pseudo-random numbers between zero and one and is commonly seeded with an index like the point number. fit remaps values from one numeric range to another; you'll often use it to convert a position range into a normalized 0-to-1 scale. The set function constructs vectors from separate floats, which is practical when you want to assign RGB values from different random calls. Together these functions let you expose artist parameters, add variety, and normalize data for driving attributes. A simple pattern is to ch a scale, use fit to remap a coordinate to a 0–1 blend, and feed that into a color calculation seeded with rand. Remember to type your attributes correctly when using these functions: fit returns a float, set produces a vector, and ch returns the parameter type you requested on the node.

Control flow in VEX lets you branch logic and perform internal repetitions. The if/else statement allows you to change attributes only when certain conditions hold, such as coloring points red when their Y position is above a threshold and blue otherwise. This is especially powerful when combined with fit or other remapping functions to create bands or ramps. Loops, like for loops, are less common at the per-element level because the wrangle itself iterates across elements, but they are useful within a single execution for tasks like averaging or sampling neighboring elements. For instance, you might loop a fixed number of times to accumulate nearby attributes into an average and then write that average to a custom attribute. A key misconception is thinking you must loop over all points; instead, plan whether the wrangle should run per point and do inner loops only for local aggregation. Always be careful with loop bounds to avoid expensive or unintended work on large geometries. Structuring conditions and internal loops with clear comments and small, predictable ranges keeps VEX fast and maintainable. Beginners often encounter a few recurring issues. One is forgetting the at symbol when referencing attributes; without it you reference a local variable instead of the attribute, producing wrong results or undefined behavior. Another common error is mixing types — for example assigning a float to a vector attribute. Always ensure you provide the correct shape: colors need vectors, while scalars require float or int types. A third issue is Run Over mismatch: if your code expects per-point context but the node is running over primitives, attributes like @P won't be meaningful. Debugging strategies include using the Geometry Spreadsheet to inspect attribute existence and types, inserting temporary attributes with clear names to confirm intermediate values, and creating ch channels to test parameter changes without editing code. When a random seed doesn't change results as expected, try offsetting the seed or adding a ch('seed') parameter. Finally, comment your VEX and test small, incremental changes rather than large rewrites. These habits reduce errors and make it easier to identify whether a problem is a type, scope, or logic error. VEX is fast, but performance still matters on large geometry sets. Avoid unbounded loops inside a per-element wrangle; looping over all points in each point execution duplicates work and multiplies cost. Prefer built-in functions which are optimized, and limit attribute writes to only those you need because every written attribute consumes memory and can slow later processing. Use temporary attributes for debugging but remove or hide them in final setups. When sampling neighbors, restrict the neighborhood size or use dedicated nodes for heavy topology queries rather than naive loops. Reuse computed values within a single execution instead of recomputing them. If you need global aggregates, perform them in a detail wrangle that runs once rather than in every point. Finally, test with smaller data sets and check timings before moving to full-resolution geometry; small prototypes reveal algorithmic issues faster than large runs. Following these steps keeps your procedural tools interactive and reliable in production pipelines. Let's summarize the essentials. First, VEX is a compact, fast language for writing per-element operations; it shines when you need procedural control over large geometry sets. Second, the Attribute Wrangle SOP runs your VEX across a chosen class—points, primitives, vertices, or detail—so match Run Over to the attributes you intend to access. Third, the at-prefixed attributes and typed declarations like f@, v@, i@ are how you read, write, and create attributes reliably. Fourth, ch, rand, fit, and set are practical functions for creating controllable parameters, seeded randomness, remapping ranges, and assembling vectors. Fifth, use the Geometry Spreadsheet and visualization SOPs to verify attribute existence and types. Finally, follow modular, small-wrangle patterns, avoid unbounded loops, expose only necessary channels, and comment your code to keep networks maintainable. These concepts give you a practical toolkit for building procedural effects that are controllable, debuggable, and efficient.
